paragraphs: Rami bar Tamrei, namely Rami bar Dikulei, of Pumbedita. He came to Sura on the eve of Yom Kippur. Everyone discarded their udders; he took them and ate them. They brought him before Rav Hisda, who asked, ‘Why did you do this?’ He answered, ‘I am from Rav Yehudah's place, where they eat them.’ He told him, ‘They impose upon him the stringencies of the place,’ etc. He answered, ‘I ate them outside the boundary.’ He said, etc. He saw that he did not wear tefillin and asked why, etc. He answered, ‘I have an intestinal illness; Rav Yehudah said one is exempt.’ He saw that he did not attach tzitzit strings and asked why. He answered, ‘It is a borrowed cloak; Rav Yehudah said it is exempt for all thirty days.’ Meanwhile they brought a man who did not honor his father and mother, and bound him. He told them, ‘Release him: whenever a positive commandment's reward is stated beside it, the earthly court is not charged with enforcing it.’ He said, ‘I see that you are very sharp-witted.’ He replied, ‘Had you been in Rav Yehudah's place, I would have shown you my sharpness’: Hullin 110a–b. Yet Menahot 29, beginning of b, has Ra'ami bar Tamrei, father-in-law of Rami bar Dikulei: the vav of va-yaharog broke, and he came before R' Zeira. Rami bar Dikulei said that Shmuel said: Yevamot 80a.
